record.title: Human screen takeover (safety override) can block behind an untimed agent GUI exec holding gui_lock while the in-container X server is unresponsive
record.description: Agent GUI tools (screenshot/click/type/key) run through AgentBox._run_tool, which acquires desktop.gui_lock(sid) and calls SandboxManager._x -> docker exec_run (scrot/xdotool) with no container-side timeout wrapper -- unlike exec (timeout -k 5), read_file and outbox_read (timeout -k 2 30), which bound their execs container-side. takeover and handback acquire the same plain threading.Lock via `with`, with no acquisition deadline. If the X server stops answering while an agent GUI exec is outstanding, that exec blocks inside the held lock and the human takeover -- the safety override meant precisely for a misbehaving screen -- cannot proceed until the exec returns; later takeover/handback/end_desktop calls queue behind it. Source chain fully verified at the cited lines; gui_lock is a plain threading.Lock (desktop.py:155-158). The decisive reproduction is the PARENT's, not mine (I cannot run Docker): parent-live l1_takeover.py created a real desktop sandbox, SIGSTOP'd Xvfb (uid desktop=1001), issued an agent screenshot whose _x scrot hung while holding gui_lock, then started a takeover thread -- l1_takeover.out shows 'takeover returned within 20s: False elapsed 20.0' and that takeover and the screenshot both completed only after SIGCONT. This confirms the serialization and that the exec/lock block the human override for at least the stall duration. It does NOT establish (a) that a prompt-injected agent, using only its own capabilities, can itself drive X into the unresponsive/grabbed state (the parent used an owner SIGSTOP, not an agent action), nor (b) that the hang is truly unbounded rather than capped near the docker SDK client timeout (docker.from_env() default ~60s, sandbox.py:286), which would raise a ReadTimeout and release gui_lock after ~60s; parent-live only measured to 20s before resuming X. Both are decisive and require the live Docker daemon plus agentbox-desktop:0.1.
record.claimed_root_cause: gui_lock is held across SandboxManager._x exec_run with no container-side timeout wrapper (unlike exec/read_file/outbox_read, which use `timeout -k`), and takeover/handback acquire the same plain threading.Lock unconditionally with no acquisition deadline, so a hung GUI exec serializes the human safety override behind it.

trace.description: Lowest-trust agent token POSTs a GUI tool (screenshot/click/type/key) to /sandboxes/{sid}/tools/{tool}, dispatched on tool_pool.
For GUI tools, acquires `with self.desktop.gui_lock(sid):` and runs the GUI method while holding it.
Runs c.exec_run(argv, user=desktop, ...) for scrot/xdotool with no container-side `timeout -k` wrapper, so the exec blocks for as long as X is unresponsive.
Human takeover (safety override) acquires the same gui_lock via a plain `with` (no deadline) and cannot return until the hung GUI exec releases it.

evidence.description: `with self.desktop.gui_lock(sid):` wraps the entire GUI tool execution in _run_tool.
_x returns c.exec_run(argv, user=DESKTOP_USER, environment=DESKTOP_ENV, demux=True) with no `timeout -k` wrapper.
By contrast, exec wraps argv in a container-side `timeout -k 5 <t>`; read_file (561) and outbox_read (665) use `timeout -k 2 30` -- _x has no equivalent bound.
self.client = docker.from_env(): the SDK client timeout (~60s default) may cap the _x exec hang and release gui_lock via a ReadTimeout, so 'indefinite' is unproven.
handback also acquires gui_lock via a plain `with`, unconditionally and with no acquisition deadline.
takeover acquires gui_lock with the inline comment that it waits until the running GUI tool finishes -- no timeout/409 path.
gui_lock(sid) returns self._gui.setdefault(sid, threading.Lock()) -- a plain threading.Lock acquired only via `with` (no timeout) everywhere it is used.
`as_desktop Xvfb :0 ...` runs the X server as uid 1001 (desktop), the same account as GUI-launched programs.

blockers: Whether a prompt-injected agent, using only its own agent-token capabilities (screenshot/click/type/key executed as uid 1001 desktop, and exec as uid 1000 agent), can itself drive the in-container X server into an unresponsive or grabbed state so that a subsequent _x scrot/xdotool exec hangs -- in agentbox-desktop:0.1. Parent-live l1_takeover.py induced the stall with an owner-side `kill -STOP` on Xvfb, not an agent action, so attacker-triggerability of the hang is unproven and needs the live Docker daemon and desktop image.

Whether the _x exec hang is truly unbounded (indefinite takeover lockout) or is capped by the docker SDK client timeout (docker.from_env() default ~60s, sandbox.py:286), which would raise a ReadTimeout and release gui_lock after ~60s (distinguishing a permanent lockout from a repeatable ~60s safety-override outage). Parent-live measured only to 20s before resuming X, so the ceiling past 60s is unobserved; needs the live daemon and image.

validation_plan.local: Disposable desktop sandbox on a real Docker daemon with agentbox-desktop:0.1 (loopback only, dummy tokens): (1) Attacker-trigger test -- with the agent token only, attempt to make a subsequent GUI exec hang using agent-reachable means (e.g. drive type/key into a terminal running as uid 1001 to issue an X server grab or saturate the X request queue) rather than an owner SIGSTOP; issue one agent screenshot, then POST takeover from a UI session and record whether it returns before the agent action is undone. (2) Bound test -- repeat the parent's SIGSTOP(Xvfb) setup but let the agent exec and the takeover block run past 90s before SIGCONT, recording whether exec_run raises a ReadTimeout near 60s and releases gui_lock (bounded ~60s, repeatable) or blocks indefinitely (permanent lockout). Keep all runs disposable and bounded. Fix check: wrap _x argv in a container-side `timeout -k 2 N` exactly as exec/read_file/outbox_read do, and have takeover/handback use gui_lock.acquire(timeout=...) returning 409/503 on contention so the human override is never serialized unboundedly behind an agent GUI exec.
